scenes.name: hook
scenes.text: Water alone can't wash off oily grime. Add a little soap, and it slides right away. What is soap doing?

scenes.name: molecule
scenes.text: A soap molecule has two ends. A head that loves water, and a long tail that hates water but loves oil.

scenes.name: micelle
scenes.text: The tails dig into oil and grime, and the molecules surround it in tiny balls called micelles.

scenes.name: germs
scenes.text: Many viruses and bacteria have a fatty outer layer. Soap tails wedge into it and can break it apart.

scenes.name: rinse
scenes.text: The water loving heads face outward, so running water carries the micelles, and the dirt, down the drain.

scenes.name: twenty
scenes.text: Scrubbing for about twenty seconds gives soap time to reach every gap, like between fingers and under nails.

scenes.name: made
scenes.text: Soap is made by reacting fats or oils with a strong alkali. This process is called saponification.

scenes.name: outro
scenes.text: Grab the oil, break the germs, rinse it away. Follow for more on how things really work.
